Whilst studying abroad in Canada I stumbled across Here comes everybody:The Power of Organizing Without Organizations by Clay Shirky. The book was about crowd sourcing before the term crowd sourcing had been created and it inspired my dissertation.

It led me to read other books on the subject of the internet like The Wealth of Networks by Yochai Benkler, the Long Tail by Chris Anderson and crowd sourcing by Jeff Howe.

In particular here comes everybody discussed the birthday paradox and how it related to internet connections birthday paradox

e.g if there are 2 people there are two possible connections, with 4 people 6 possible connections but with 10 people there are 45 possible connections, now imagine that each connection is a person on the internet and they make a post which appeals to several people who post it to their other connections, thats how things go viral in its most basic form.

What other books had an impact on your way of thinking? What do you recommend reading?
What was the most significant (to you) non fiction book you've read?

The Age of the Economist by Daniel R. Fusfeld is awesome. It isn't a huge book, but it packs a lot of good information about the history of economic theory. It starts with some agrarian trade and moves forward to the modern day federal reserve and world bank. It was my text book for an intro econ class I took a few years ago, and I still love it.

The Denial of Death by Ernest Becker. Also, the Bhagavad Gita.

Flash Boys by Michael Lewis; the author of Moneyball. Very short book where Lewis discusses the Wall Street's role in the economic collapse. Specifically how high-frequency trading gave Wall Street an unfair advantage in the Stock Market when high-frequency trading was first introduced.
'Rich Dad, Poor Dad' changed my financial perspective.

Persecution and the Art of Writing by Leo Strauss.

People invariably roll their eyes if you so much as mention the term "esoteric writing" but Strauss has contributed massively to the way I approach texts, has changed how I think about censorship and has given me a lot to think about regarding responsible teaching.
I always liked Cosmos by Carl Sagan. Some of the science in it is a bit dated now but it's a very enjoyable read for a non-fiction book.
